sections.content: Sometimes you mention a doubt or a difficulty and then want to say that it does not change what follows. *De todos modos*, *de todas formas* and *en cualquier caso* ("anyway", "in any case") do this: they put the doubt aside and go back to what stays true or what you will do. *De todas formas* is the most everyday; *en cualquier caso* sounds a little more careful.

sections.title: The doubt first, then what holds
rows: No sé si hará buen tiempo; de todos modos, saldremos.
I do not know if the weather will be good; anyway, we will go out.
Puede que Meg llegue tarde; en cualquier caso, empezamos a las ocho.
Meg may be late; in any case, we start at eight.
No sé si me contestarán; de todas formas, voy a escribir.
I do not know if they will answer me; anyway, I am going to write.

sections.content: The doubt comes before the marker and what holds comes after it. You know *sin embargo* from A2 Unit 28: it sets two facts against each other, while *de todos modos* says that the first one does not change the second. Do not swap them.
